title: Co-opt or Coexist? A Study of Medical Cannabis Dispensaries' Identity-Based Responses to Recreational-Use Legalization in Colorado and Washington
abstract: When recreational cannabis dispensaries first entered the U.S. market in 2014, how did incumbent medical cannabis dispensaries react? Did they emphasize their distinct identity as medical providers, distancing themselves from recreational dispensaries and those consumers who consume cannabis recreationally? Or did they downplay their medical orientation to compete directly for potential resources? In this study, we propose that how incumbent organizations position their identities in response to increasing competition from an emerging rival form depends on key audiences' acceptance of the new form. Using data on the evolving cannabis markets in the states of Colorado and Washington during the year following the initial emergence of the recreational category, we find a sharpening of identity among medical dispensaries in communities with low voter support for recreational-use legalization. Medical dispensaries accentuated the medical orientation of their identities as recreational dispensaries increasingly set up operations and as buyers inclined more toward recreational use. In contrast, we find a blurring of medical/recreational identity in communities where voters demonstrated support for recreational-use legalization.
summary_en: When recreational cannabis became legal in Colorado and Washington in 2014, incumbent medical-cannabis dispensaries faced a strategic dilemma: emphasise their distinct medical identity or blur with the new recreational segment. Using detailed dispensary-level data from the year following legalisation, Hsu, Koçak and Kovács show that the response varied with local audience attitudes. In communities where voters had supported recreational legalisation, medical dispensaries blurred their identity; in communities with low voter support, they sharpened it. Identity strategy depends on which audience the firm prioritises.
data_used: Dispensary-level identity claims (descriptions, marketing, product mix) for cannabis dispensaries in Colorado and Washington over the year following recreational-use legalisation in 2014, matched to county-level recreational-use ballot outcomes.
policy_relevance: When deregulation creates new firm types, regulators often assume incumbents will compete by lowering quality (race to the bottom) or by exiting. The paper shows incumbents instead reshape identity claims, with the direction depending on local public attitudes. Relevant for Hungarian regulators handling deregulation in pharmacy chains, alternative medicine, or other professional services where identity boundaries matter for licensing.
